summary: Creates a registry of collation methods, the rules for comparing and sorting strings. Sorting international text is hard and outside the IETF's expertise, so protocols can refer to named collations here.

plainLanguage.summary: Different languages sort letters differently. Instead of every protocol inventing its own order, this sets up a list of named sorting rules that protocols can point to.

questions: how do protocols sort international strings
how do i register a collation with iana
subtitle: A registry of named string-comparison rules, so protocols can say exactly how text is matched and sorted.

tldr.problem: Many protocols search, match or sort strings, but comparing international text well is a large problem outside the IETF's expertise.
tldr.mechanism: A collation is a named function that compares two strings. RFC 4790 defines how collations are named, what they must specify, how protocols should use them, and an IANA registry that holds them, seeded with three collations.
tldr.outcome: Protocols can point to a collation by identifier instead of defining comparison rules themselves, and new collations can be added later without changing the protocols.

today: RFC 4790 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Collation Registry
sections.content:
The Application Configuration Access Protocol (ACAP, RFC 2244) introduced a similar idea called a comparator, but never created an IANA registry for it. With stringprep and the Unicode Collation Algorithm now available, RFC 4790 creates that registry and fills it with some initial values. It replaces and generalizes the ACAP comparator definition.

The abstract is candid about the scope: searching and sorting international strings is large, not fully explored and outside the IETF's expertise. So the RFC builds an abstraction framework in which protocols identify a comparison function precisely, and the set of functions can grow.
sections.plainLanguage: Sorting words correctly in every language is very hard. So this RFC does not try to solve it. It just builds a shelf where experts can put their sorting rules, each with a name.

sections.title: What a Collation Is
sections.content:
A collation is a named function that takes two strings of any length and can perform up to three operations: an equality test, a substring match and an ordering test. The point is separation of concerns. Someone with the right expertise defines the comparison, and any number of protocols can use it. The RFC compares this to how a charset separates character mapping from a protocol like MIME, or how SASL separates authentication mechanisms from a protocol like ACAP.

Protocols such as IMAP and ACAP search can therefore just specify how they plug into the registry, rather than listing every collation they support. The RFC uses client, server and protocol loosely: a Sieve interpreter running a user's script counts as a server, and the Sieve language counts as a protocol.

A collation may turn each string into a sort key first, which can be an identity mapping or something unreadable to a human. That is an implementation detail, and a protocol SHOULD NOT expose sort keys to clients because implementations use different formats.
sections.plainLanguage: A collation is a rulebook for deciding whether two words are the same and which comes first. Giving each rulebook a name means any program can say "use that one".

sections.title: Collation Identifiers
sections.content:
A collation identifier is a single US-ASCII string of at most 254 characters, built from letters, digits, hyphens, semicolons, equals signs and full stops. The special identifier default refers to a protocol's default collation; for protocols without one it MUST match no collations.

A client choosing a collation may use wildcard characters (an asterisk), which match zero or more collation characters and MUST NOT be adjacent. If several collations match, the server SHOULD prefer a widely useful one. For ordering, an identifier may be prefixed with a plus sign (no effect) or a minus sign (reverse the result). Protocols that use URIs rather than tokens can use a reserved section of the IANA URL space.

The naming guidelines are advisory. International collations typically start with i;, language-specific ones with a language tag and a semicolon, followed by the algorithm and modifications. Table versions SHOULD appear as parameters. Names of the form vnd-hostname in the second position (between semicolons) are reserved for vendor collations created by the owner of that hostname.
sections.plainLanguage: Each rulebook gets a short label, like a library call number. You can also ask for "anything starting with this", and you can flip the order by putting a minus sign in front.

sections.title: What a Collation Must Specify
sections.content:
A collation specification MUST state which of the three operations it supports and how to perform them on any two strings, including empty ones. Collations must be deterministic: the same identifier and the same two strings must always give the same result. For any single collation, either none or all of its operations can return undefined.

Every collation also provides a validity test, which is true when a string is equal to itself under the collation. It is not listed in registrations. Equality returns match or no-match for valid input and MUST be reflexive and symmetric, and transitive for valid input. A collation with a substring or ordering test MUST also have an equality test, and they must agree.

Substring asks whether the first string occurs within the second under the collation's equality. It can match strings of unequal length, such as a pre-composed and a decomposed accented character, so position information SHOULD give both start and end offsets. Ordering returns less, equal, greater or undefined and MUST be reflexive, and transitive and trichotomous for valid input.

A specification SHOULD describe how it builds sort keys. Collations with more than one customizable lookup table MUST assign numbers to those tables so that clients and servers can use the same ones.
sections.plainLanguage: A good rulebook must always give the same answer for the same two words, and it must say which questions it can answer: are they the same, does one contain the other, and which comes first.

sections.title: What Protocols Using Collations Must Do
sections.content:
A protocol that searches, matches or sorts non-ASCII text has to be clear about which characters, not just octets, the collations apply to, for example by fixing UTF-8. It must say which operations can be invoked and MUST give the client a way to choose a collation. If it allows wildcards in identifiers, it MUST say what happens with no negotiation or with default, and SHOULD provide a way to list matching collations.

If a protocol needs a total ordering and a collation returns undefined, the recommended fallback is to sort invalid strings after valid ones, ordering them with i;octet. The RFC also suggests that protocols consider specific error codes for no matching collation, an unsupported operation and errors in matching.

The text notes that case-insensitive comparison may differ by language, since a server might treat "i" and "I" as equivalent in Italy and different in Turkey. Clients that work offline may not be able to reproduce a server's collation if it uses configurable tables, and the RFC leaves a table-download mechanism out because the problem is not yet well understood.

In the informative section on existing protocols, ACAP and Sieve used collations before this registry and do not meet every requirement. IMAP's built-in comparison is explicit only with the COMPARATOR extension, and in IMAP the default collation is i;ascii-casemap.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs that use these rulebooks have to say which letters they are using, let people pick a rulebook, and decide what to do when a word does not fit any rule. Some languages need different rules, so one size does not fit all.

sections.title: How Collations Are Registered
sections.content:
Registration starts when a completed XML template is sent to IANA and to the collation@ietf.org list, which the IETF creates for public discussion. The IESG appoints a designated expert who is expected to answer within two weeks: approved, approved with minor changes, or rejected with cause. Decisions can be appealed to the IESG Applications Area Director and then the IESG.

The registration document's collation element carries a scope of global, local or other, and an intendedUse of common, limited, vendor or deprecated. Required child elements are identifier, title, operations, specification and owner. A submitter is needed unless the owner element holds an email address, and a version element is required if the registration is likely to be revised. An optional variable element controls behavior such as case sensitivity.

IANA stores each document under the collation's identifier and keeps a text summary with four sections: common, limited, vendor and deprecated. The expert is encouraged to reject "common" registrations that should be "limited", to keep that list small and of high quality. Example reasons to reject include badly formed XML, a vague specification, an identifier that does not pin down table versions, and failing a MUST in the requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: To add a new rulebook to the shelf, you fill in a form and send it in. One expert checks it within about two weeks and says yes, yes with small changes, or no with a reason.

sections.title: The Three Initial Collations
sections.content:
The RFC registers three collations that were first defined in ACAP and are implemented in most Sieve engines. It admits some behavior is not ideal, such as i;ascii-casemap accepting non-ASCII input, but compatibility with widely deployed code won.

  • i;ascii-numeric compares arbitrarily large unsigned decimal numbers stored as octet strings. Input is cut at the first non-digit; a string that does not start with a digit stands for positive infinity. It supports equality and ordering but not substring. For example, "4294967298", "04294967298" and "4294967298b" are all equal.
  • i;ascii-casemap works on octet strings and ignores case for US-ASCII letters by changing lower-case letters (octet values 97-122) to upper case (65-90) first. It does not treat non-ASCII letters case-insensitively and is not suited to natural language: it can mis-sort names with accents or words like "Lloyd", which sorts after "Lyon" in Welsh.
  • i;octet is a simple, fast comparison of binary octet strings, roughly memcmp with length checks. It never returns undefined, is usable only by protocols that explicitly allow it, and compares unsigned octet values from 0 to 255.
sections.plainLanguage: The first three rulebooks are very simple: one sorts numbers by value, one ignores capital letters for plain English letters only, and one just compares raw bytes one at a time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Collations will normally be used with UTF-8 strings, so the RFC says the security considerations for UTF-8, stringprep and Unicode TR-36 also apply and are normative for this specification. The RFC adds no further security mechanism of its own. A registration can also be rejected if the specification it references does not adequately address security considerations specific to that collation.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the rulebooks mostly compare text, the safety warnings for handling text in other documents apply here too.

data.title: Collation registration template
data.code:
<?xml version='1.0'?>
<!DOCTYPE collation SYSTEM 'collationreg.dtd'>
<collation rfc="YYYY" scope="global" intendedUse="common">
  <identifier>collation identifier</identifier>
  <title>technical title for collation</title>
  <operations>equality order substring</operations>
  <specification>specification reference</specification>
  <owner>email address of owner or IETF</owner>
  <submitter>email address of submitter</submitter>
  <version>1</version>
</collation>
